question:
A 61-year-old African American male presents to his primary care physician reporting leg swelling that
started approximately two weeks ago without any identifiable trigger. He also mentions joint pain,
headaches, frothy urine, and tingling in his fingers and toes, though he does not believe these
symptoms are related to the swelling. He denies shortness of breath, back pain, or skull pain. His
medical history includes well-controlled rheumatoid arthritis, diabetes, and hypertension. On physical
examination, there is 3+ pitting edema in both legs. A chest radiograph shows mild cardiac
enlargement. Urinalysis reveals 3+ proteinuria and casts with a cross-like appearance under polarized
light. Renal biopsy demonstrates a characteristic finding visible only under polarized light. Which of the
following is most associated with the likely cause of this patient’s edema? Answer Choices: (A)
Elevated levels of IL-6 (B) Elevated levels of hemoglobin A1c (C) Antibodies to phospholipase A2
receptor (D) Increased serum TNF-alpha levels (E) Abnormally shaped red blood cells (F) Elevated
serum complement levels (G) Decreased serum albumin with normal globulins (H) Anti-nuclear
antibodies with homogeneous pattern (I) Altered kappa to lambda ratio (J) Elevated rheumatoid factor
titers
 A. Antibodies to phospholipase A2 receptor
B. Elevated levels of hemoglobin A1c
C. Abnormally shaped red blood cells
D. Elevated rheumatoid factor titers
E. Decreased serum albumin with normal globulins
F. Anti-nuclear antibodies with homogeneous pattern
G. Altered kappa to lambda ratio
H. Elevated serum complement levels
I. Increased serum TNF-alpha levels
J. Elevated levels of IL-6
